planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil; site both a male and female plant nearby if fruit set is wanted, since this species is dioecious.

directions: Native to woodland margins of central and southern China, Taiwan, and the Philippines, this compact evergreen viburnum carries small glossy leaves marked with three prominent veins, closely related to the better-known Viburnum davidii. Flat clusters of small white flowers open in spring, and because plants are dioecious, only female plants pollinated by a nearby male will set the small blue-black fruit that follows in fall. Grow in evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, sheltering from harsh winter wind in its coldest hardiness range. Its dense, rounded habit needs little pruning beyond removing occasional wayward shoots to keep a tidy outline.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in fertile, well-drained soil where late-winter flowers will be visible from indoors.

directions: Collected from open Himalayan forest from Afghanistan east to Assam, this sparse, gnarled deciduous shrub produces unusually large rounded flower clusters for a viburnum, with buds that are deep pink before opening to a lighter pink-flushed white on bare branches in late winter and early spring. The scented flowers are followed by berries that ripen from red through to black, eaten readily by birds and, in its native range, by Asiatic black bears. It is the direct parent, along with Viburnum farreri, of the popular hybrid Viburnum x bodnantense. Grow in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil, and prune only to remove old or crossing wood immediately after flowering so next season's bloom buds are not lost.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in cool, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil, mimicking the understory conditions of its native mountain forests.

directions: A close relative of the eastern North American hobblebush, this large deciduous shrub grows wild in cool mountain forests of Japan, Korea, and Taiwan and bears flattened, lacecap-style clusters of white flowers in late spring, with small outer florets ringing a center of tiny fertile blooms. Bold, rounded leaves with a bronze cast when young mature to deep green and turn shades of red and purple in autumn, and the summer flowers give way to small fruit that ripens from red to black. Plant in cool, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture in partial shade, since it resents hot, dry sites; a woodland edge planting suits its naturally broad, open habit best. Established plants need only light removal of dead or damaged wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil; propagate increase stock from softwood cuttings taken in early summer.

directions: First collected in northwest Yunnan, China, and introduced into Western cultivation by the plant hunter George Forrest in 1920, this compact shrub has since earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliable garden performance. Pointed, toothed leaves set off clusters of star-shaped flowers in white to bright pink, opening in early to midsummer after most other deutzias have already finished. Grow in moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and renew the shrub after flowering by removing a portion of the oldest stems at ground level to keep new flowering wood coming on. Increase stock from softwood cuttings taken in early summer.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
